title: Stripe Payments vs PayPal Checkout
summary: A developer-first payment platform versus a wallet-led checkout with broad buyer familiarity; in both cases your business generally remains the seller.
recommendation: Choose Stripe as the primary stack when APIs, payment-method breadth, and modular billing matter. Add or choose PayPal when buyer wallet preference and PayPal conversion are central. Many businesses support both rather than treating the decision as exclusive.

differences.first: Composable payments infrastructure and developer tooling.
differences.second: A familiar buyer wallet and PayPal-branded checkout.
differences.whyItMatters: The right primary option depends on your buyers and required integration depth.

differences.second: PayPal Checkout is listed at 3.49% + $0.49, with separate card rates.
differences.whyItMatters: Compare the exact payment method, not the company-level headline.

differences.first: Checkout, Elements, Payment Links, mobile SDKs, and APIs.
differences.second: PayPal Checkout and Expanded Checkout with different customization and risk options.
differences.whyItMatters: Implementation effort and merchant control differ.

differences.first: Stripe Billing is a separate priced product with extensive lifecycle APIs.
differences.second: PayPal provides subscriptions and recurring-payment APIs.
differences.whyItMatters: Model lifecycle requirements before selecting a subscription stack.

differences.first: Your business owns tax, disputes, and product support.
differences.second: Your business remains seller; eligible PayPal protections have conditions.
differences.whyItMatters: Neither standard product is a general Merchant of Record.

implementation.summary: Stripe has the simpler no-code starting point through Payment Links, but its production surface expands with the amount of control selected. A standard PayPal Checkout integration is narrower but normally spans browser buttons plus server-side order creation and capture; subscriptions add a separate catalog and webhook lifecycle.

first.label: No code
first.detail: Create and share a Payment Link for one-time or recurring payments without application code.

second.label: Copy and paste
second.detail: PayPal advertises a short button integration, but a production standard flow connects the browser SDK to server endpoints.

first.label: Variable
first.detail: Payment Links are no-code; hosted Checkout is low-code; Elements and PaymentIntents trade more code for more control.

second.label: Client + server
second.detail: The JavaScript SDK renders buttons while the server creates and captures Orders using protected credentials.

first.label: Separate product
first.detail: Stripe Billing adds subscription models, lifecycle APIs, a hosted portal, and webhook-driven access sync.

second.label: Separate API flow
second.detail: PayPal Subscriptions uses catalog products, billing plans, JavaScript buttons, REST APIs, and subscription webhooks.

first.label: Webhook sync
first.detail: Your application verifies events and fulfills only after the relevant payment or invoice succeeds.

second.label: Webhook sync
second.detail: Alternative methods and subscriptions require handling approved, pending, completed, denied, and lifecycle events correctly.

first.label: Broad toolkit
first.detail: Sandboxes, CLI, test clocks, SDKs, Workbench, and detailed guides across several integration paths.

second.label: Focused toolkit
second.detail: Developer dashboard, sandbox buyer and business accounts, JavaScript and server SDKs, samples, and webhook tools.

first.label: Adaptive
first.detail: Checkout can dynamically present cards, wallets, Link, and eligible local methods in a merchant-branded flow.

second.label: Wallet led
second.detail: A familiar PayPal approval experience emphasizes PayPal balance, Pay Later, Venmo where eligible, and guest cards.

first.label: Low to extensive
first.detail: Choose limited hosted-page styling or build a highly customized embedded payment experience.

second.label: Option dependent
second.detail: Standard Checkout uses PayPal buttons and approval UI; Expanded Checkout offers more card-form control and configuration.

first.label: Merchant owned
first.detail: The merchant operates tax, disputes, product support, reconciliation, and the selected billing stack.

second.label: Merchant owned
second.detail: The merchant remains seller and owns tax and product operations; PayPal protections apply only to eligible transactions.

scenarios.when: You are building an API-driven SaaS billing stack.
scenarios.reason: Its modular payments and Billing APIs are the stronger center of gravity.

scenarios.when: Your audience explicitly asks for PayPal or prefers wallet balances.
scenarios.reason: Buyer familiarity can matter more than a small fee difference.

scenarios.when: You serve a mixed consumer audience.
scenarios.reason: Use Stripe as the primary card stack and evaluate PayPal as an additional method rather than forcing a false either-or choice.
